newsitem.title: GERMANY: Call for German tax action falls on deaf ears.
newsitem.headline: Call for German tax action falls on deaf ears.

text.p: An appeal by a leading German economist to step up the pace of tax reforms fell on deaf ears on Thursday as politicians blamed each other over the breakdown of cross-party talks.

Rolf Peffekoven, who sits on the "five wise men" panel of economic advisers, said the quicker that planned tax cuts worth 30 billion marks ($17.8 billion) are passed, the sooner Germany can make inroads into its record post-war unemployment.

If Finance Minister Theo Waigel can push through proposals for sweeping cuts in corporate taxes in 1998 and 1999, German corporate giants which racked up big profit gains last year would invest less abroad and create more jobs at home, he said.
"Something must happen on this front," Peffekoven told ZDF public television.

Despite the wise man's exhortations, the Easter deadline set by the Bonn coalition to reach a compromise on tax reforms with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) was set to expire with no deal -- and not even talks -- in sight.
Repeating recent accusations, coalition leaders mocked SPD leader Oskar Laftontaine's demand for top-level talks with Chancellor Helmut Kohl to get negotiations restarted.

"Lafontaine has no interest in getting results, so we must go ahead and legislate," Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), told German radio. "He is pursuing a scorched-earth policy."

Michael Glos, parliamentary leader of Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU), said Lafontaine's spoiling tactics -- aimed at getting "a ripe plum to fall into his lap" at next year's general election -- would fail.

SPD chief whip Peter Struck replied his party was not ready to talk to Waigel alone, saying the coalition reforms contained a time bomb which would blow a 50 billion mark hole in the budget just as Europe's single currency is launched in 1999.
"Kohl must take personal charge of the issue. He is, after all, the head of the government," Struck said. "He can't just send in the second team."

The coalition has already introduced its 1998 tax bill into parliament, which would cut the main corporate tax rate to 40 percent from 47 percent and cut two points off the 7.5 percent solidarity surcharge levied to aid eastern Germany.
The real row centres, however, on big income tax cuts which would come in a second round of coalition legislation for 1999.
The SPD opposes plans to cut top-rate income tax, wants a drop in income tax for ordinary workers from 1998 and wants Germany's high labour insurance to be slashed this summer.
With the SPD able to block tax measures in parliament's upper house, politicians will still have to seek compromise later this year in parliament's lengthy mediation process.

Whether Germany can afford the wait looks increasingly doubtful after some of the country's top economic institutes warned that high unemployment could knock billions of marks off projected tax revenues this year.

The Kiel-based IfW institute said that tax revenues would fall 15 billion marks short of the numbers on which the 1997 budget was based. The next revenue estimates, which are compiled by an independent commission, are due in May.
IfW economist Alfred Boss said he expected the budget deficit to be 3.3 percent of GDP, above the Maastricht Treaty's three percent ceiling which Waigel has vowed to meet.
Other institutes polled by the Berliner Zeitung newspaper also expect shortfalls. A three percent deficit works out at 110 billion marks, based on official forecasts.
Waigel said last weekend that welfare cuts and even tax increases could be needed to balance the books and enable Germany to join European monetary union (EMU).

But FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt said Bonn should not insist on fulfilling the deficit target exactly because Germans would refuse to pay more to join EMU. "People won't be prepared to pay a special tax for the euro," he told the Spiegel weekly in an article released ahead of publication this weekend.
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097 150 ($ = 1.681 German Marks)
